# Part 1. Introduction and Research Questions

## 1.1 Background
Two people can walk away from the same conversation with different impressions of how it went. Perceived interaction quality refers here to a person's subjective evaluation of a particular interaction, including how engaging, smooth, natural, comfortable, and positive it felt.
This project examines whether nine questionnaire items can be represented by a common perceived interaction quality factor and whether conversation partners' latent evaluations are associated.

## 1.2 Research Questions
**RQ1.** How well does a one-factor measurement model account for responses to the perceived interaction quality items?

**RQ2.** To what extent are conversation partners' latent evaluations of interaction quality associated?

**RQ3.** Are the findings sensitive to allowing a residual covariance between QI8 and QI9 or removing these two items?

## 1.3 Expectations and Analytic Approach
Because both partners experienced the same conversation, their evaluations may be positively associated.
Three measurement specifications are examined:
**1.** An initial nine-item one-factor model.
**2.** A nine-item model allowing a residual covariance between QI8 and QI9.
**3.** A seven-item model excluding QI8 and QI9.

The seven-item model is an exploratory sensitivity analysis motivated by discussion of item content. QI8 and QI9 explicitly assess comfort and positive feelings. However, the distinction between these items and QI1–QI7 is not absolute: QI3 also assesses enjoyment.
Model selection is not based on obtaining the largest partner correlation.

## 1.4 Dataset
The dataset includes 218 participants across 46 sessions, with ratings from both partners for 412 conversations. Within each session, participants spoke with multiple partners in a round-robin design. Each conversation contributed two sets of ratings, and each participant could contribute ratings for several conversations.

**Note.** The data were provided by Dr. Erin Heerey's lab and are restricted to course use. The analysis code documents how the data were prepared and analyzed.

## 1.5 Conceptual Dyadic Model

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-conceptual-model
%%| fig-cap: "Conceptual dyadic measurement model."
flowchart TB
    A(("Partner A perceived<br/>interaction quality"))
    B(("Partner B perceived<br/>interaction quality"))
    A <--> B
    A --> IA["Partner A item responses"]
    B --> IB["Partner B item responses"]
```

# Part 2. Data Preparation and Validation
## 2.1 Load Packages and Import Data
```{r}
#| label: setup
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(psych)
library(gt)
library(lavaan)
library(ggplot2)
library(semPlot)

options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE)

piq_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  "piq_scored_all.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## 2.2 Define Variables and Analysis Helpers
Separate item lists are retained so that the seven-item sensitivity analysis does not overwrite the nine-item analysis.
```{r}
#| label: define-variables
qi_items_9 <- paste0("QI", 1:9)
qi_items_7 <- paste0("QI", 1:7)
id_columns <- c(
  "StudySessionID",
  "ConversationNum",
  "PID",
  "ptrID"
)

required_columns <- c(id_columns, qi_items_9)

missing_columns <- setdiff(
  required_columns,
  names(piq_raw)
)

if (length(missing_columns) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "Required columns are missing: ",
    paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

fit_indices <- c(
  "chisq", "df", "pvalue",
  "cfi", "tli", "rmsea",
  "rmsea.ci.lower", "rmsea.ci.upper",
  "srmr"
)

fit_row <- function(fit, label) {
  values <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, fit_indices)

  tibble::as_tibble_row(as.list(values)) |>
    mutate(
      Model = label,
      N = as.integer(lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "nobs")),
      .before = 1
    )
}

show_fit <- function(table) {
  table |>
    gt::gt() |>
    gt::cols_label(
      N = "Records",
      chisq = "Chi-square",
      df = "df",
      pvalue = "p",
      cfi = "CFI",
      tli = "TLI",
      rmsea = "RMSEA",
      rmsea.ci.lower = "90% CI lower",
      rmsea.ci.upper = "90% CI upper",
      srmr = "SRMR"
    ) |>
    gt::fmt_integer(columns = c(N, df)) |>
    gt::fmt_number(
      columns = chisq,
      decimals = 2
    ) |>
    gt::fmt_number(
      columns = c(
        pvalue, cfi, tli, rmsea,
        rmsea.ci.lower, rmsea.ci.upper, srmr
      ),
      decimals = 3
    ) |>
    gt::sub_missing(missing_text = "—")
}

partner_correlation <- function(fit) {
  unname(
    lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv")[
      "quality_A", "quality_B"
    ]
  )
}

fmt3 <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.3f", x)
}

fmt2 <- function(x) {
  sprintf("%.2f", x)
}

fmt_p <- function(x) {
  if (is.na(x)) {
    return("p unavailable")
  }

  if (x < .001) {
    return("p < .001")
  }

  paste0("p = ", sprintf("%.3f", x))
}

fit_text <- function(fit) {
  x <- lavaan::fitMeasures(fit, fit_indices)

  paste0(
    "χ²(", as.integer(x["df"]), ") = ",
    fmt2(x["chisq"]), ", ",
    fmt_p(x["pvalue"]),
    ", CFI = ", fmt3(x["cfi"]),
    ", TLI = ", fmt3(x["tli"]),
    ", RMSEA = ", fmt3(x["rmsea"]),
    ", 90% CI [",
    fmt3(x["rmsea.ci.lower"]), ", ",
    fmt3(x["rmsea.ci.upper"]), "]",
    ", SRMR = ", fmt3(x["srmr"])
  )
}

check_fit <- function(fit) {
  if (!isTRUE(lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "converged"))) {
    stop("A model did not converge. Inspect it before interpreting results.")
  }

  invisible(fit)
}
```

## 2.3 Select IDs and Item Responses
The scored QI values are used as supplied. No additional reverse scoring is applied in this analysis. The scoring of negatively worded items QI3, QI5, and QI7 should be documented using the laboratory's scoring procedures.

```{r}
#| label: select-data
piq_dat <- piq_raw |>
  select(all_of(required_columns))

numeric_items <- vapply(
  piq_dat[qi_items_9],
  is.numeric,
  logical(1)
)

if (!all(numeric_items)) {
  stop("All QI items must be numeric before analysis.")
}

glimpse(piq_dat)
```

## 2.4 Check ID Completeness and Self-Ratings
```{r}
#| label: check-ids
id_check <- piq_dat |>
  summarise(
    rating_records = n(),
    missing_session = sum(is.na(StudySessionID)),
    missing_round = sum(is.na(ConversationNum)),
    missing_PID = sum(is.na(PID)),
    missing_partner = sum(is.na(ptrID)),
    self_ratings = sum(PID == ptrID, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

id_check |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "ID and Rating-Record Checks"
  )

if (anyNA(piq_dat[id_columns])) {
  stop("Missing IDs must be resolved before matching partners.")
}

if (any(piq_dat$PID == piq_dat$ptrID)) {
  stop("Self-ratings were found. Resolve them before matching partners.")
}
```

## 2.5 Check Duplicate Directed Ratings
A directed rating is one participant's evaluation after a conversation with a specific partner.

```{r}
#| label: check-duplicates
#| include: false
duplicate_ratings <- piq_dat |>
  count(
    StudySessionID,
    ConversationNum,
    PID,
    ptrID,
    name = "n_records"
  ) |>
  filter(n_records > 1L)

tibble(
  Check = "Duplicate directed-rating keys",
  Count = nrow(duplicate_ratings)
) |>
  gt::gt()

if (nrow(duplicate_ratings) > 0L) {
  print(duplicate_ratings)

  stop(
    "Duplicate directed ratings were found. ",
    "Resolve them before reshaping."
  )
}
```

## 2.6 Check Item Ranges and Missing Responses
The questionnaire response scale ranges from 1 to 7.

```{r}
#| label: check-item-values
#| include: false
item_check <- piq_dat |>
  select(all_of(qi_items_9)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Item",
    values_to = "Response"
  ) |>
  group_by(Item) |>
  summarise(
    Nonmissing = sum(!is.na(Response)),
    Missing = sum(is.na(Response)),
    Missing_percent = mean(is.na(Response)) * 100,
    Outside_1_to_7 = sum(
      !is.na(Response) &
        (Response < 1 | Response > 7)
    ),
    Noninteger = sum(
      !is.na(Response) &
        abs(Response - round(Response)) > 1e-8
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

item_check |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Item Range and Missingness Checks"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = Missing_percent,
    decimals = 2
  )

if (
  any(item_check$Outside_1_to_7 > 0L) ||
  any(item_check$Noninteger > 0L)
) {
  stop("Unexpected QI response values were found.")
}
```

## 2.7 Summarize Item Responses
```{r}
#| label: item-descriptives

item_descriptives <- piq_dat |>
  select(all_of(qi_items_9)) |>
  psych::describe() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Item") |>
  select(
    Item, n, mean, sd, median,
    min, max, skew, kurtosis
  )

item_descriptives |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Item Descriptive Statistics",
    subtitle = "Perceived interaction quality"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    n = "N",
    mean = "M",
    sd = "SD",
    median = "Median",
    min = "Min",
    max = "Max",
    skew = "Skewness",
    kurtosis = "Kurtosis"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(mean, sd, median, skew, kurtosis),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "N represents nonmissing rating records,",
      "not independent participants."
    )
  )
```
Item means ranged from 4.98 (QI5) to 5.87 (QI1, QI7, and QI8), indicating that participants generally evaluated their conversations positively. QI5 had the lowest mean and the largest standard deviation (SD = 1.65), suggesting more variability in perceived awkward pauses than in the other items. All items were negatively skewed, which is consistent with many responses near the upper end of the 1–7 scale. This ceiling pattern is one reason the continuous-ML treatment is described as a limitation. QI9 had slightly fewer nonmissing responses (N = 819) than the other items, but missingness was minimal for all items.

# Part 3. Preliminary One-Factor CFA
## 3.1 Purpose and Estimation
The preliminary models examine the item measurement structure before partners' responses are modeled jointly. This is a diagnostic step rather than a required prerequisite for every dyadic CFA.

These models pool individual rating records and do not account for repeated participation or reciprocal ratings. Their fit statistics and standard errors are therefore interpreted as preliminary.

For consistency with the original analyses, all models use maximum likelihood estimation, treat the seven-category items as continuous (1 = Strongly disagree , 7 = Strongly agree), and use full-information maximum likelihood for missing item responses. Factor variances are fixed to one using `std.lv = TRUE`.

## 3.2 Test 1: Initial Nine-Item Model
```{r}
#| label: fit-individual-nine

qi_model1 <- "
  perceived_interaction_quality =~
    QI1 + QI2 + QI3 + QI4 + QI5 +
    QI6 + QI7 + QI8 + QI9
"

qi_fit1 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_model1,
  data = piq_dat,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_fit1)

summary(
  qi_fit1,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 3.3 Inspect Potential Local Misfit
Modification indices are diagnostic information, not an automatic rule for adding parameters.

```{r}
#| label: individual-nine-mi

lavaan::modindices(qi_fit1) |>
  filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs) |>
  arrange(desc(mi)) |>
  select(lhs, op, rhs, mi, epc, sepc.all) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Largest Residual-Covariance Modification Indices",
    subtitle = "Initial nine-item CFA"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(mi, epc, sepc.all),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

## 3.4 Test 2: Nine-Item Model With QI8–QI9 Residual Covariance
QI8 assesses comfort and QI9 assesses positive feelings (MI = 57.653). Their content provides a possible rationale for shared variation beyond the general interaction quality factor.
This model modification is exploratory because it was considered after examining the initial model.

```{r}
#| label: fit-individual-nine-residual

qi_model2 <- "
  perceived_interaction_quality =~
    QI1 + QI2 + QI3 + QI4 + QI5 +
    QI6 + QI7 + QI8 + QI9

  QI8 ~~ QI9
"

qi_fit2 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_model2,
  data = piq_dat,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_fit2)

summary(
  qi_fit2,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 3.5 Test 3: Seven-Item Sensitivity Model
The seven-item model excludes QI8 and QI9 to examine whether the measurement results depend on including these items.

```{r}
#| label: fit-individual-seven

qi_model3 <- "
  perceived_interaction_quality =~
    QI1 + QI2 + QI3 + QI4 + QI5 +
    QI6 + QI7
"

qi_fit3 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_model3,
  data = piq_dat,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_fit3)

summary(
  qi_fit3,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 3.6 Summarize Preliminary Model Fit
```{r}
#| label: individual-fit-table

individual_fit_table <- bind_rows(
  fit_row(
    qi_fit1,
    "Test 1: Nine-item one-factor CFA"
  ),
  fit_row(
    qi_fit2,
    "Test 2: Nine-item CFA with QI8–QI9 residual covariance"
  ),
  fit_row(
    qi_fit3,
    "Test 3: Seven-item one-factor CFA"
  )
)

individual_fit_table |>
  show_fit() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Preliminary One-Factor CFA Results"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Seven- and nine-item models contain different indicators.",
      "Their fit indices are presented descriptively;",
      "they are not treated as a conventional nested-model comparison.",
      "Rows represent individual rating records."
    )
  )
```
The initial nine-item model yielded `r fit_text(qi_fit1)`. Allowing the QI8–QI9 residual covariance improved CFI and reduced RMSEA, although RMSEA remained elevated. Excluding these two items did not consistently improve fit across indices. Thus, the revised nine-item model was retained for further examination of its factor loadings.

## 3.7 Inspect Standardized Factor Loadings

```{r}
#| label: individual-loadings

individual_models <- list(
  "Test 1: Nine items" = qi_fit1,
  "Test 2: Nine items + residual covariance" = qi_fit2,
  "Test 3: Seven items" = qi_fit3
)

individual_loadings <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(individual_models), function(label) {
    lavaan::standardizedSolution(
      individual_models[[label]]
    ) |>
      filter(op == "=~") |>
      transmute(
        Model = label,
        Item = rhs,
        Standardized_loading = est.std
      )
  })
)

individual_loadings |>
  gt::gt(groupname_col = "Model") |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Standardized Factor Loadings"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = Standardized_loading,
    decimals = 3
  )
```
All items loaded positively and substantially on the single factor. In Test 2, standardized loadings ranged from .499 (QI3) to .878 (QI2). QI2 (smooth and coordinated) and QI4 (natural) were the strongest indicators, whereas QI3 (did not enjoy the interaction) was the weakest. The two items considered for removal, QI8 and QI9, had loadings of .701 and .733, higher than those of QI3, QI6, and QI7. Therefore, the psychometric evidence does not suggest that these items are poor indicators of the common factor. The estimated QI8–QI9 residual covariance was .145 (standardized = .287), indicating a modest amount of shared variance beyond the general factor.

# Part 4. Construct the Dyadic Dataset
## 4.1 Assign Partner Labels
A and B denote the lower and higher participant IDs within a pair. These are organizational labels, not theoretically distinct roles.
A conversation is identified by its session, conversation round, and the two participant IDs. Multiple pairs may converse during the same session and round.

```{r}
#| label: assign-partner-labels

piq_pair_long <- piq_dat |>
  mutate(
    A_ID = pmin(PID, ptrID),
    B_ID = pmax(PID, ptrID),
    member = if_else(PID == A_ID, "A", "B")
  )
```

## 4.2 Check Reciprocal Pair Completeness
The code stops if a conversation does not have exactly one A rating record and one B rating record. Missing item responses within a record are handled separately by FIML.
```{r}
#| label: check-reciprocal-pairs

pair_check <- piq_pair_long |>
  group_by(
    StudySessionID,
    ConversationNum,
    A_ID,
    B_ID
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_records = n(),
    n_A = sum(member == "A"),
    n_B = sum(member == "B"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pair_check |>
  count(n_records, n_A, n_B, name = "Conversations") |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Reciprocal Pair Completeness"
  )

incomplete_pairs <- pair_check |>
  filter(
    n_records != 2L |
      n_A != 1L |
      n_B != 1L
  )

if (nrow(incomplete_pairs) > 0L) {
  print(incomplete_pairs)

  stop(
    "Some conversations do not have exactly one rating per partner. ",
    "Review these records before continuing."
  )
}
```
All 412 conversations contained exactly one rating record from each partner, allowing all conversations to be retained in the dyadic dataset.

## 4.3 Reshape to One Row per Conversation
All nine items are retained in the wide dataset. The seven-item models simply omit QI8 and QI9 from their model syntax.

```{r}
#| label: reshape-dyads

piq_dyad <- piq_pair_long |>
  select(
    StudySessionID,
    ConversationNum,
    A_ID,
    B_ID,
    member,
    all_of(qi_items_9)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      StudySessionID,
      ConversationNum,
      A_ID,
      B_ID
    ),
    names_from = member,
    values_from = all_of(qi_items_9),
    names_glue = "{.value}_{member}"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    StudySessionID,
    ConversationNum,
    A_ID,
    B_ID
  )

stopifnot(
  nrow(piq_dyad) == nrow(pair_check),
  nrow(piq_dat) == 2L * nrow(piq_dyad)
)

glimpse(piq_dyad)
```

## 4.4 Summarize the Analytic Sample
Participants are counted using session–participant combinations, allowing for the possibility that ID codes are reused across sessions.

```{r}
#| label: sample-summary

n_rating_records <- nrow(piq_dat)

n_participants <- piq_dat |>
  distinct(StudySessionID, PID) |>
  nrow()

n_sessions <- n_distinct(piq_dat$StudySessionID)

n_conversations <- nrow(piq_dyad)

sample_summary <- tibble(
  Unit = c(
    "Individual rating records",
    "Participants (session–PID combinations)",
    "Sessions",
    "Reciprocally matched conversations"
  ),
  N = c(
    n_rating_records,
    n_participants,
    n_sessions,
    n_conversations
  )
)

sample_summary |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Analytic Sample"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns = N)
```

The dataset contains `r n_rating_records` rating records from `r n_participants` participants across `r n_sessions` sessions, representing `r n_conversations` reciprocally matched conversations.
Participants could contribute ratings for multiple conversations. Thus, neither individual rating records nor conversation-level rows are necessarily independent.
The data were provided by Dr. Erin Heerey's lab and are restricted to course use.

# Part 5. Fit the Dyadic CFA Models
## 5.1 Dyadic Measurement Structure
Each model estimates one perceived interaction quality factor for Partner A and one for Partner B.
The factor covariance is freely estimated. With factor variances fixed to one, it also represents the latent correlation.
Measurement parameters are estimated separately for A and B. Equality constraints across partners are not imposed in these exploratory models.

## 5.2 Model D1: Initial Nine-Item Dyadic CFA
```{r}
#| label: fit-dyadic-nine

qi_dyad_model1 <- "
  quality_A =~
    QI1_A + QI2_A + QI3_A + QI4_A + QI5_A +
    QI6_A + QI7_A + QI8_A + QI9_A

  quality_B =~
    QI1_B + QI2_B + QI3_B + QI4_B + QI5_B +
    QI6_B + QI7_B + QI8_B + QI9_B

  quality_A ~~ quality_B
"

qi_dyad_fit1 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_dyad_model1,
  data = piq_dyad,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_dyad_fit1)

summary(
  qi_dyad_fit1,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 5.3 Inspect QI8–QI9 Correlation Residuals
Here, a correlation residual is the observed correlation minus the model-implied correlation. It is not the estimated correlation between two item error terms.
Positive values indicate that the model underestimates the corresponding observed item association.

```{r}
#| label: dyadic-correlation-residuals

dyadic_residuals <- lavaan::lavResiduals(
  qi_dyad_fit1,
  type = "cor"
)

qi89_correlation_residuals <- tibble(
  Partner = c("A", "B"),
  Item_pair = c(
    "QI8_A and QI9_A",
    "QI8_B and QI9_B"
  ),
  Correlation_residual = c(
    dyadic_residuals$cov["QI8_A", "QI9_A"],
    dyadic_residuals$cov["QI8_B", "QI9_B"]
  )
)

qi89_correlation_residuals |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "QI8–QI9 Correlation Residuals",
    subtitle = "Initial nine-item dyadic CFA"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = Correlation_residual,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Observed correlation minus model-implied correlation.",
      "These values are not estimated error correlations."
    )
  )
```
The initial dyadic model underestimated the QI8–QI9 association for both partners, with correlation residuals of .145 for Partner A and .071 for Partner B. Together with the items’ shared emphasis on comfort and positive feelings, this pattern motivated an exploratory model allowing a separate QI8–QI9 residual covariance for each partner.

## 5.4 Model D2: Nine-Item Dyadic CFA With Residual Covariances
A separate QI8–QI9 residual covariance is estimated within each partner.
These paths do not connect Partner A's item errors to Partner B's item errors.

```{r}
#| label: fit-dyadic-nine-residual

qi_dyad_model2 <- "
  quality_A =~
    QI1_A + QI2_A + QI3_A + QI4_A + QI5_A +
    QI6_A + QI7_A + QI8_A + QI9_A

  quality_B =~
    QI1_B + QI2_B + QI3_B + QI4_B + QI5_B +
    QI6_B + QI7_B + QI8_B + QI9_B

  quality_A ~~ quality_B

  QI8_A ~~ QI9_A
  QI8_B ~~ QI9_B
"

qi_dyad_fit2 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_dyad_model2,
  data = piq_dyad,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_dyad_fit2)

summary(
  qi_dyad_fit2,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 5.5 Model D3: Seven-Item Dyadic CFA
QI8 and QI9 are excluded from both partners' factors. No QI8–QI9 residual covariance is included because these items are not part of this model.

```{r}
#| label: fit-dyadic-seven

qi_dyad_model_7 <- "
  quality_A =~
    QI1_A + QI2_A + QI3_A + QI4_A + QI5_A +
    QI6_A + QI7_A

  quality_B =~
    QI1_B + QI2_B + QI3_B + QI4_B + QI5_B +
    QI6_B + QI7_B

  quality_A ~~ quality_B
"

qi_dyad_fit_7 <- lavaan::cfa(
  model = qi_dyad_model_7,
  data = piq_dyad,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "ML",
  std.lv = TRUE
)

check_fit(qi_dyad_fit_7)

summary(
  qi_dyad_fit_7,
  standardized = TRUE,
  fit.measures = TRUE,
  rsquare = TRUE
)
```

## 5.6 Compare Dyadic Model Fit
```{r}
#| label: dyadic-fit-table

dyadic_fit_table <- bind_rows(
  fit_row(
    qi_dyad_fit1,
    "D1: Nine-item dyadic CFA"
  ),
  fit_row(
    qi_dyad_fit2,
    "D2: Nine-item dyadic CFA with residual covariances"
  ),
  fit_row(
    qi_dyad_fit_7,
    "D3: Seven-item dyadic CFA"
  )
)

dyadic_fit_table |>
  show_fit() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Dyadic CFA Model Fit"
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Records represent conversations.",
      "Seven- and nine-item specifications use different indicators;",
      "comparisons across these item sets are descriptive.",
      "Dependence across conversations has not been modeled."
    )
  )
```
D2 yielded `r fit_text(qi_dyad_fit2)`. Compared with D1, allowing the within-partner QI8–QI9 residual covariances increased CFI and TLI and reduced RMSEA. The seven-item model showed no consistent advantage across fit indices. D2 was therefore selected as the primary exploratory specification, retaining all nine items while accounting for the additional QI8–QI9 association.


## 5.7 Compare Partner Latent Correlations
The partner latent correlation describes the association between partners' overall latent evaluations. It does not measure exact agreement in their response levels.

```{r}
#| label: partner-correlations

partner_r_table <- tibble(
  Model = c(
    "D1: Nine-item dyadic CFA",
    "D2: Nine-item dyadic CFA with residual covariances",
    "D3: Seven-item dyadic CFA"
  ),
  Partner_latent_r = c(
    partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit1),
    partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit2),
    partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit_7)
  )
)

partner_r_table |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Partner Latent Correlations"
  ) |>
  gt::cols_label(
    Partner_latent_r = "Partner latent r"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = Partner_latent_r,
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = paste(
      "Similar point estimates do not establish statistical equivalence.",
      "Correlations are interpreted conditional on each measurement model."
    )
  )
```
The partner latent correlation was `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit1))` in D1, `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit2))` in D2, and `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit_7))` in D3. The estimates changed little across specifications, suggesting that the positive association was not driven solely by QI8 and QI9. Across conversations, partners who evaluated their interaction more positively tended to have partners who also evaluated it more positively.

## 5.8 Inspect Remaining Local Misfit
Large modification indices identify potential model limitations. Additional paths are not automatically added on the basis of these values.

```{r}
#| label: revised-dyadic-mi

lavaan::modindices(qi_dyad_fit2) |>
  filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs) |>
  arrange(desc(mi)) |>
  select(lhs, op, rhs, mi, epc, sepc.all) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Remaining Potential Local Misfit",
    subtitle = "Revised nine-item dyadic CFA"
  ) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(mi, epc, sepc.all),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

# Part 6. Visualize the Findings
## 6.1 Observed Partner Mean Scores
The figure uses the nine-item observed means. It is a descriptive visualization, not a plot of the latent factor estimates.
Means are calculated from available items. The number of available items can vary across rating records.

```{r}
#| label: fig-partner-scores
#| fig-cap: "Observed nine-item mean scores for both partners. Each point represents one conversation; the dashed line marks equal observed means."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.5

partner_scores <- piq_dyad |>
  mutate(
    mean_A = rowMeans(
      as.matrix(
        pick(all_of(paste0(qi_items_9, "_A")))
      ),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mean_B = rowMeans(
      as.matrix(
        pick(all_of(paste0(qi_items_9, "_B")))
      ),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    is.finite(mean_A),
    is.finite(mean_B)
  )

ggplot(
  partner_scores,
  aes(x = mean_A, y = mean_B)
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    colour = "grey50"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = .40,
    colour = "#216869",
    size = 2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 1:7
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 1:7
  ) +
  coord_fixed(
    xlim = c(1, 7),
    ylim = c(1, 7)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Partner A observed mean QI score",
    y = "Partner B observed mean QI score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```
Most conversations received relatively positive evaluations, with many partner mean scores between 5 and 7. The point cloud showed an overall positive trend, suggesting that partners’ evaluations tended to vary together. However, many points fell away from the equality line, indicating that partners sometimes experienced the same conversation differently.

```{r}
#| label: model-selection-summary

chisq_d1 <- unname(lavaan::fitMeasures(qi_dyad_fit1, "chisq"))
chisq_d2 <- unname(lavaan::fitMeasures(qi_dyad_fit2, "chisq"))
df_d1 <- unname(lavaan::fitMeasures(qi_dyad_fit1, "df"))
df_d2 <- unname(lavaan::fitMeasures(qi_dyad_fit2, "df"))

chisq_diff_d1_d2 <- chisq_d1 - chisq_d2
df_diff_d1_d2 <- df_d1 - df_d2
p_diff_d1_d2 <- pchisq(
  chisq_diff_d1_d2,
  df = df_diff_d1_d2,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

selection_table <- dyadic_fit_table |>
  select(Model, chisq, df, cfi, tli, rmsea, srmr) |>
  mutate(Partner_latent_r = partner_r_table$Partner_latent_r)

selection_table |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::tab_header(title = "Dyadic Model Selection Summary") |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = chisq, decimals = 2) |>
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(cfi, tli, rmsea, srmr, Partner_latent_r),
    decimals = 3
  )
```

# Part 7. Results, Interpretation, and Limitations
## 7.1 Selection of the Final Model
D2, the nine-item dyadic model with separate QI8–QI9 residual covariances for each partner, was selected as the primary exploratory model for four reasons.
First, D2 fit better than D1, which uses the same nine items without the residual covariances. CFI and TLI increased, RMSEA and SRMR decreased, and the chi-square difference was 355.29 (df = 132, p < .001).
Second, D2 matched or modestly outperformed the seven-item model. CFI and TLI were essentially the same, whereas RMSEA and SRMR were lower for D2. Because the seven- and nine-item models contain different indicators, this comparison is descriptive.
Third, QI8 and QI9 were substantial indicators of the common factor. Removing them reduced the content coverage of the scale without producing a clearly better measurement model.
Fourth, the partner latent correlation was nearly unchanged across D1, D2, and D3, so the decision does not depend on obtaining a larger correlation.
D2 is described as acceptable rather than excellent: CFI was just below .95, RMSEA was in the acceptable range, and some local misfit remained. Because the model was modified after examining the data and does not account for dependence across conversations, it is treated as an exploratory final model rather than a confirmed measurement model.

## 7.2 Preliminary Measurement Results
The initial nine-item one-factor model yielded `r fit_text(qi_fit1)`. Allowing a residual covariance between QI8 and QI9 yielded `r fit_text(qi_fit2)`. The seven-item sensitivity model yielded `r fit_text(qi_fit3)`. In the current results, allowing the QI8–QI9 residual covariance improved the descriptive fit of the nine-item model. Removing QI8 and QI9 did not produce a consistent improvement across fit indices. Because the seven- and nine-item models contain different observed indicators, their fit indices are interpreted descriptively rather than as a conventional nested-model comparison. Improved fit does not, by itself, establish that the revised model adequately captures every aspect of the item relationships.

## 7.3 Dyadic Measurement Results
The initial nine-item dyadic model yielded `r fit_text(qi_dyad_fit1)`. The revised nine-item dyadic model, including separate QI8–QI9 residual covariances within each partner, yielded `r fit_text(qi_dyad_fit2)`. The seven-item dyadic model yielded `r fit_text(qi_dyad_fit_7)`. These dyadic fit results must be evaluated separately from the preliminary individual-record CFA results.

## 7.4 Partner Latent Association
The estimated partner latent correlation was `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit1))` in the initial nine-item dyadic model, `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit2))` in the revised nine-item model, and `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit_7))` in the seven-item model. The seven-item estimate differed from the initial nine-item estimate by `r fmt3(partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit_7) - partner_correlation(qi_dyad_fit1))`. In the current results, these similar point estimates suggest that the positive association between partners' latent evaluations was not driven solely by QI8 and QI9. This finding concerns association rather than exact agreement. A positive correlation indicates that partners' evaluations tend to vary together across conversations; it does not imply identical ratings or equal average levels. The sensitivity analysis does not establish statistical equivalence between the correlations, and changes in the point estimates are not treated as evidence of statistically significant differences.

## 7.5 Interpretation of QI8 and QI9
QI8 and QI9 may both reflect general interaction quality while also sharing additional content related to comfort and positive feelings. Allowing a residual covariance acknowledges shared variation not captured by the general factor. It does not establish that the additional variation represents a distinct positive-affect factor or identify its cause. The seven-item analysis provides an alternative operationalization with narrower item coverage. Its results are useful for evaluating sensitivity to item inclusion, not for choosing whichever specification produces the largest partner correlation.

## 7.6 Limitations
First, participants contributed ratings to multiple conversations within sessions. The current dyadic models represent dependence between the two partners in a conversation through their factor covariance, but they do not account for dependence across conversations arising from repeated participants or shared sessions. Fit statistics, standard errors, and population-level inference therefore remain preliminary.
Second, A and B are assigned by participant ID rather than by theoretically meaningful roles. Separate measurement parameters are estimated for each position. These models do not establish exchangeability or measurement equivalence across partners. Partner equality constraints and the implications of the labeling scheme require further consideration.
Third, the seven-category item responses are treated as continuous under maximum likelihood estimation. Analyses using an ordinal-data estimator could be considered as an additional sensitivity analysis, with appropriate attention to differences in missing-data handling and model estimation.
Fourth, the QI8–QI9 residual covariance and seven-item specification were examined after inspecting the data and discussing item content. These analyses are exploratory and would benefit from evaluation in an independent sample.
Finally, the latent partner association is conditional on the specified measurement model. Remaining local misfit, omitted cross-partner item associations, or other measurement assumptions may affect its interpretation.
